catalog_quote: § 25. The accentuation in native ME. words was essentially the same as in OE., that is, in all uncompounded words the chief accent fell upon the stem-syllable and always remained there even when suffixes and inflexional endings followed it. In compound words the chief accent fell upon the stem-syllable of the first component part if the second part was a noun or an adjective; and on the stem-syllable of the second part if this was a verb or derived from a verb. ... § 186. The O.Fr. and AN. accented vowels in early borrowed words, which became post-tonic in ME. through shifting of the accent, remained for a time unchanged, and then later became weakened down through loss of the new secondary accent ... § 215. The O.Fr. and AN. pretonic vowels and diphthongs which became tonic (accented) through the shifting of the accent generally remained in ME.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Middle English carries an empty rule; this work supplies the placement (stem-initial / leftmost-foot main stress, continuing Old English) and the loanword exceptions, consistent with the 'morphological' kind our list of works to obtain assigns to the record.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Middle English kept the Old English (Germanic) stress system: main stress on the stem-initial syllable regardless of syllable weight (certain prefixes unstressed), with Germanic Feet built left to right and main stress on the leftmost foot; the Old-to-Middle English changes (Final Destressing, Final Consonant Extrametricality, Trisyllabic Shortening) did not move main stress, they only shortened words metrically. Directionality and main-stress position did not change before 1530.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress built from left to right by Germanic Feet (ms. p.2 (1)); Old English (and by continuity ME) 'lacked secondary stress in final syllables' (ms. p.8, (15)); Final Destressing / Final Consonant Extrametricality account for the lack of final secondary stress in the transition to ME (ms. p.9, (16)-(17)).
new_statements.exceptions: Romance loans could show French stress (final, or penult if final is schwa) in Chaucer's verse, but 'could in general also be stressed according to the native English pattern, as required by the meter', giving doublets citee ~ citee, comfort ~ comfort, divers ~ diverse, geaunt ~ geant, Plato ~ Plato, present ~ present (ms. p.5 (7)); PDE reflexes of these words have initial stress 'with very few exceptions' (degree, divine, reward: ms. p.5); the authors reject Halle & Keyser's (1971) claim that a Romance stress rule entered English in Chaucer's time (ms. pp.6-7).
new_statements.identity_note: Dresher & Lahiri 2005 is explicitly about early Middle English (title) with loan data from Chaucer's late-14th-century London English; Dresher 2013 and Dresher & Lahiri 2022 cover the whole ME period to c.1530/1570; Wardale is a general ME handbook with no dialect restriction. No source describes a specific ME dialect's stress as differing.

new_statements.quote: Stress in West Germanic and in Old English invariably falls on the first syllable of the word, unless the word is prefixed, in which case the prefix is stressed in nouns, but not in verbs. [p.3] ... Although the changes sketched above had a dramatic effect on nominal paradigms, they had no effect on the position of main stress, and the stress system in Middle English remained essentially as in Old English. [...] Both Old English and Middle English had stress on the root-initial syllable, regardless of quantity. Feet were built iteratively from left to right, resulting in secondary stressed feet in longer words, which, however, were becoming increasingly rare. [p.24]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Middle English (catalog-all-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; this work supplies the placement: root-initial main stress regardless of quantity, Germanic resolved moraic trochee, left-to-right parsing, secondary stress on later feet but not on final syllables, loans nativised. Nothing in the catalog is contradicted. It also matches the companion Dresher & Lahiri papers already held by the project in this folder (2005 'Main stress left in early Middle English'; 2022 'The foot in the history of English').
new_statements.rule_in_words: Middle English kept the Old English (West Germanic) system: main stress on the first syllable of the root, independent of syllable weight ('Main stress: Left'); the foot is the Germanic resolved/expanded moraic trochee parsed left to right. Unstressed prefixes fall outside the main-stress position in verbs (OE nouns stress the prefix, verbs do not; native outputs like begin keep root stress). Romance loans into Middle English were nativised to this system (comparable 1413, residence 1386 parsed leftward, main stress left) rather than importing French/Latin stress; the authors find no evidence the Old French or Latin stress rule took hold at the time of Chaucer. Per their chronology (26): 1400 foot direction leftward, main stress left (as in OE); c.1530 direction rightward but main stress still left (severity, rarity); c.1660 main stress right (early Modern English, Latinate pattern: heavy penult else antepenult with final extrametricality).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Iterative left-to-right Germanic feet gave secondary stresses on non-initial feet in longer words (all heavy syllables except one following an initial light syllable expected to be footed); final syllables carried no secondary stress ('Recall that final syllables did not have secondary stress, a fact we accounted for in the earlier period by defooting (3), and in the later period by consonant extrametricality (CEM) (4)', p.24). Many OE/ME suffixes are stress-neutral and outside the stress domain; metrical shortenings (HVD, TSS, CEM) reduced most native ME words to a single foot, so secondary-stress feet were increasingly rare.
new_statements.exceptions: Prefixed words: prefix stressed in nouns but not in verbs (OE ge- unstressed; stress on the root). Stress-neutral suffixes excluded from the domain. Romance loans in ME follow native prosodic preferences (OSL/TSS quantity alternations vane~vanity) with main stress left; only from c.1530 do long Latinate loans with suffixes -ation, -ic(al), -ity, -ator, -able/-ible show rightward parsing, and from c.1660 French suffixes -eer, -ee, -ade, -esque, -ette, -oon retain final main stress -- these fall in early Modern English, after the ME period proper.
new_statements.identity_note: The chapter spans West Germanic/Old English through early Modern English; its Middle English statements are general (not dialect-specific) and cover both native vocabulary and Romance loans into ME (OED first-attestation dates 1230-1560 cited). The stress-shift stages dated 1530 and 1660 belong to early Modern English, not to Middle English (midd1317).

tone_statements.quote: Metrical rules are always relative, in some way, to language. The tonal patterns of Tang poetry can’t be applied as such to English, because it has no phonologised tones to pattern. Conversely, Tang verse provides an important body of metrical evidence for the tones of Middle Chinese, and the specific tones of the particular lexemes used in verse.

sources.quote: Metrical rules are always relative, in some way, to language. The tonal patterns of Tang poetry can’t be applied as such to English, because it has no phonologised tones to pattern. Conversely, Tang verse provides an important body of metrical evidence for the tones of Middle Chinese, and the specific tones of the particular lexemes used in verse.

sources.note: A rebuttal of Schipper's Englische Metrik on Middle English word accent and the Germanic long line, argued from King Horn and La3amon rather than from imitations of foreign metres; syllables are classed as hochtonig / tieftonig / tonlos (primary-stressed, secondary-stressed, unstressed - 'Ton' = stress accent), with rules for which may carry a verse lift, followed by a defence of the author's King Horn scansion and a survey of four-lift stanzaic poems. Entirely about stress placement and verse an earlier reading; nothing on pitch, tone or intonation.
